topic: Computational Design of Mercury Oxidation Catalysts: From Support Modifications to Active Site Design
title: Computational Design of Mercury Oxidation Catalysts: From Support Modifications to Active Site Design
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Mercury (Hg) emissions from fossil fuel combustion facilities pose a significant threat to the global environment due to their high toxicity and bioaccumulation potential. Catalytic oxidation of elemental Hg using heterogeneous metal oxide catalysts has emerged as an economically and catalytically efficient approach for Hg removal. In this study, we present a comprehensive investigation of mercury oxidation catalysts using an integrated computational approach combining density functional theory (DFT) calculations and advanced machine learning methodologies. We first examined how modifications to the TiO₂ support structure (crystallographic phase control and reduction treatment) affect the Hg oxidation activity of VO x /TiO₂ catalysts. We found that phase control from anatase to rutile enhanced the Hg oxidation activity, while reduction treatment decreased it due to changes in the charge density at the VO x active center. Notably, the interaction between the V site and surface Cl played a critical role in balancing two key reaction steps of HCl dissociation and HgCl₂ desorption. Then, we systematically investigated various transition metal oxide clusters (MnO₂, Fe₂O₃, CuO, CoO, MoO₃, and CeO₂) supported on TiO₂ as alternative catalysts for low-temperature mercury oxidation. For the HgCl₂ formation pathway, CeO₂/TiO₂ demonstrated superior performance, while CuO/TiO₂ exhibited enhanced activity in the HgO formation pathway. Through various electronic structure analyses, we identified key electronic descriptors for catalytic activity, including charge density of active metal centers, Fermi level position, and metal-oxygen bond strength. Throughout these studies, the relationship between electronic structure and catalytic activity was interpreted within the Sabatier principle, confirming that optimal catalytic activity requires moderate interaction strength between reactants and catalysts. These findings provide molecular-level understanding for the rational design of mercury oxidation catalysts and offer valuable guidelines for developing technologies for mercury emission control and multi-pollutant removal systems.

topic: The Influence of Nickel Dispersion and Alumina Structure on the Ammonia Decomposition
title: The Influence of Nickel Dispersion and Alumina Structure on the Ammonia Decomposition
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Hydrogen is a key alternative to fossil fuels due to its zero CO₂ emissions, but challenges in transportation limit its widespread use. Ammonia is considered a promising hydrogen carrier. Various catalysts have been studied for this process, with nickel-based catalysts standing out among non-noble metals for their low cost and favorable catalytic properties. This study focuses on investigating nickel catalysts supported on different alumina types, emphasizing how the support material impacts metal dispersion in ammonia decomposition. Different alumina was employed in 𝛾-Al 2 O 3 , θ-Al 2 O 3 , and α-Al 2 O 3 . Nickel was impregnated (10%) on the alumina supports and calcined at 450 °C. Catalyst characterizations using specific surface area (S BET ), CO chemisorption, X-ray diffraction (XRD), and temperature-programmed reduction (H 2 -TPR). Catalytic tests were carried out at temperature range of 300 to 650°C with pure NH₃. These results of XRD patterns (Figure 1) confirm the successful incorporation of nickel onto the Al₂O₃ supports. The H 2 -TPR profile (Figure 2) of Ni-based catalysts supported on alumina is characterized by three distinct peaks: α, β, and γ. These peaks correspond to the reduction of Ni species with varying metal-support interactions. The activity and reaction rate of ammonia decomposition of all catalysts a dependence on temperature (Figure 3). The 10Ni/𝛾-Al 2 O 3 catalyst exhibited the highest conversion (95%) at 550 °C, which that the 10Ni/θ-Al 2 O 3 follows with a conversion of 88.8% and 10Ni/α-Al 2 O 3 of 86.3%. These results indicate that the alumina structure of did not influence the Ni particle dispersion on consequently the activity (Table 1). The hydrogen rate production increases with temperature (Figure 3), reaching maximum rates of 60.50 mmol min -1 g -1 for 100% ammonia conversion at 600 °C. In conclusion, the catalytic performance of the activity and rate production were independent of the alumina structure and the Ni particle sizes. However, the performances depend solely on the temperature.

title: Catalytic Partial Oxidation of Biogas on Catalyst Prepared By 3-D Printing Basic Oxide Supports

abstract: Catalytic partial oxidation of biogas is a process where biogas is reacted with air in substoichiometric amounts to produce hydrogen and carbon monoxide. The process can occur at millisecond contact times over structured catalysts. Typically, reticulated foams have been used as supports, but the materials available are limited. Our lab has previously used 3-D printed ceramics as structured supports for millisecond catalytic partial oxidation and found that their performance is comparable to reticulated foams. In this work, we have had basic oxides 3-D printed for catalyst supports. The basic nature of the support has led to enhanced carbon dioxide, a prime component of biogas, adsorption and conversion in the millisecond reactor.

topic: Improved Durability of Ni/YSZ-Based Catalysts for Ammonia Cracking in Solid Oxide Fuel Cells
title: Improved Durability of Ni/YSZ-Based Catalysts for Ammonia Cracking in Solid Oxide Fuel Cells
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Ammonia (NH 3 ) has emerged as a promising hydrogen carrier due to its high gravimetric and volumetric hydrogen storage capacities, along with its carbon-free nature. Its direct utilization in solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) offers an attractive route for sustainable power generation. However, the development of robust anode catalysts for direct ammonia-fed SOFCs remains a significant challenge, particularly due to performance degradation at high operating temperatures (700–900 °C), especially under thermal cycling. One major degradation mechanism is believed to be of the anode material, which not only reduce catalytic activity but also compromise mechanical stability. In this study, we report on an enhanced Ni/YSZ-based anode catalyst with improved resistance to sintering and nitridation during ammonia decomposition at temperatures above 600 °C. The impact of surface treatment strategies on catalyst durability is also evaluated and discussed.

topic: Synthesis and Catalytic Evaluation of Ferrite-Perovskite Catalysts for CO 2 Hydrogenation to Light Olefins
title: Synthesis and Catalytic Evaluation of Ferrite-Perovskite Catalysts for CO 2 Hydrogenation to Light Olefins
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Light olefins (C 2 -C 4 = ) play a significant role in the raw materials market of the petrochemical industry. The thermocatalytic hydrogenation of CO 2 in a tandem reactor is a promising and challenging route to produce C 2 -C 4 = . However, the development of an active and selective catalyst for this process is still ongoing. Ferrites and Fe perovskites have shown promising results in CO 2 hydrogenation to C 2 -C 4 = due to their oxygen vacancies, defects and hydrogenation capacity. In this work, a series of novel ferrite-perovskite-hematite catalysts was developed, characterized and tested for CO₂ hydrogenation to light olefins. The components of the K-ZnFe 2 O 4 /LaFeO 3 /Fe 2 O 3 , K-CuFe 2 O 4 /LaFeO₃/Fe₂O₃, K-CoFe 2 O 4 /LaFeO₃/Fe₂O₃ and K-MnFe 2 O 4 /LaFeO₃/Fe₂O₃ catalysts (70/25/5 % wt) were synthesized separately via precipitation and subsequently physically mixed. Temperature programmed reduction and X-ray diffraction (XRD) were performed. Additional characterization includes CO 2 -TPD, N 2 physisorption and TGA analysis. The catalytic tests were carried out in an automated reaction system GTL Microactivity Effi PID Eng&Tech (360°C, 20 bar, WHSV: 1600 mL g -1 h -1 and H₂/CO 2 /N₂: 1:3:0.4). The results of the K-ZnFe 2 O 4 /LaFeO 3 /Fe 2 O 3 catalyst are shown in Figure 1. Overall, the three materials and final mixed catalyst exhibited high crystallinity, which evidenced the formation of ZnFe₂O₄, LaFeO₃, Fe₂O₃ structures (Figure 1A). The TPR results (Figure 1B) exhibited the reduction of different Fe species within the ferrite and perovskite structures to Fe oxides and metallic Fe. The K-ZnFe₂O₄/LaFeO₃/Fe₂O₃ catalyst (Figure 1C) showed 36.4% CO₂ and 40.8% H₂ conversions. CO and CH₄ selectivities were 13.6% and 24.2%, respectively, with total hydrocarbon selectivity of 62.2%. These results indicate effective tandem reaction performance: CO₂ reduction to CO followed by Fischer–Tropsch hydrocarbon formation through C-C coupling reaction. Light olefins were the dominant products 33.0 % (wt), mainly butene and propene. Ongoing research with the K-CuFe 2 O 4 /LaFeO₃/Fe₂O₃, K-CoFe 2 O 4 /LaFeO₃/Fe₂O₃ and K-MnFe 2 O 4 /LaFeO₃/Fe₂O₃ catalysts will assess the influence of these metals on hydrogenation capacity and the selectivity toward C 2 -C 4 = .

topic: Molecular Structure of Na-WO x /SiO₂ Catalysts Under Operating Conditions: Dispersed Vs. Crystalline Phases in Selective Methane Activation during OCM
title: Molecular Structure of Na-WO x /SiO₂ Catalysts Under Operating Conditions: Dispersed Vs. Crystalline Phases in Selective Methane Activation during OCM
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: The oxidative coupling of methane (OCM) offers a direct route to produce valuable C₂ hydrocarbons, yet the underlying catalytic mechanisms remain elusive. The Mn₂O₃-Na₂WO₄/SiO₂ system has demonstrated high activity (~30% CH₄ conversion) and selectivity (~70% C₂), but the molecular origin of active sites governing methane activation and selectivity is not well understood. This study explores the fundamental surface chemistry of Na-WOx/SiO₂ catalysts, focusing on how dispersed and crystalline Na-WOx phases influence catalytic performance. We hypothesize that dispersed Na-WOx sites selectively activate methane by forming reactive atomic oxygen species (O*), facilitating C₂H₆ formation while mitigating overoxidation. In contrast, crystalline Na₂WO₄ structures transition into a molten phase under reaction conditions, promoting molecular oxygen species (O₂*), which drive unselective oxidation pathways. To probe these effects, we systematically synthesized Na-WOx/SiO₂ catalysts via incipient wetness impregnation, enabling precise control over the ratio of dispersed Na-WOx and crystalline Na₂WO₄. In situ Raman spectroscopy elucidated molecular structures, linking surface phase composition to catalytic function measured using high resolution photoionization mass spectroscopy (PIMS) while near ambient XPS provided insights into surface elemental changes. Our findings provide fundamental insights into reaction kinetics and active site behavior in OCM, offering a rational design approach for more selective and efficient catalysts.

topic: Tuning Nanoparticle Proximity and Size: Controlling the Agglomeration Narrative of Metal/TiO 2 Nanosheet Catalytic Systems
title: Tuning Nanoparticle Proximity and Size: Controlling the Agglomeration Narrative of Metal/TiO 2 Nanosheet Catalytic Systems
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: The design of metal oxide (MO x ) supported metal nanoparticles (NP) as heterogeneous catalysts has garnered significant attention. However, the sintering of supported metal NPs has been a perennial challenge. This requires careful consideration for the choice of MO x support such as titania and modulating the physical attributes (example: size, proximity, dispersity) of NPs on the support. Here, we have developed a better synthetic protocol to fabricate Cu/TiO 2 and Fe/TiO 2 catalysts by tweaking the pathways of NP deposition. To modulate the proximity and size of nanoparticles, the synthetic protocol involves changing the physical parameters of the mother liquor, such as pH and the addition of organic ligand. The Fe and Cu NPs were successfully deposited on the titania surface, as shown in Figure 1. We have obtained a size range of 1.5-4 nm and proximity in the range of 6-12 nm for Fe NPs by varying the pH of the mother liquor. The increase in particle size and proximity is inversely proportional to the solution's pH. Further, homogeneity in the dispersion of NPs on the titania support was then modulated by the addition of a suitable amine ligand during synthesis. The standard deviation for the proximity of Fe NPs on TiO 2 was calculated to be 2.87 nm for the modified protocol (Fe/TiO 2 _M) (Figure 1 F) against the standard deviation of 3.37 nm for Fe NPs on TiO 2 NS in case of unmodified protocol (Fe/TiO 2 _U) (Figure 1 E). A comparable increase in the oxygen vacancies on the TiO 2 nanosheet surface was observed in the O1s spectrum of the XPS analysis data, in case of modified TiO 2 support which supports the enhanced Fe deposition TiO 2 NS. In summary, this investigation helps establish control over the size, proximity, and distribution of metal on TiO 2 systems which is key to increase their effective catalytic lifetime.

topic: Hydrocracking of PVC-Mixed Polyolefin (PO) over Bifunctional Tungsten-Carbide (W x C) Catalysts
title: Hydrocracking of PVC-Mixed Polyolefin (PO) over Bifunctional Tungsten-Carbide (W x C) Catalysts
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: The global plastic waste crisis continues to escalate due to the widespread use of polyolefins (POs) in packaging, consumer goods, and industrial applications. Most of the polyolefin plastic waste remains unprocessed, leading to environmental pollution and inefficient resource utilization. Hydrocracking converts polyolefins into valuable hydrocarbons using bifunctional catalysts that combine metallic sites for (de)hydrogenation and acid sites for carbon-carbon bond scission. The reaction faces issues in catalyst deactivation by poly-vinyl chloride (PVC) in mixed plastics and slow polymer diffusion between metallic and acidic active sites. This study explores tungsten-carbide (W x C) catalysts as an efficient, PVC-compatible, cost-effective alternative to noble-metal/zeolite hydrocracking catalysts. Characterization results revealed that with rising carburization temperature ( T carb ), W/W₂C phases that provide “metallic” function are formed (Fig. a). An initial increase followed by a decrease in acidic sites is observed, alongside a continuous rise in metallic sites (Fig. b-c). Kinetic studies show that as T carb increases, the reaction rate exhibits a volcano-shaped curve explained by the requirement of balance between metallic and BAS (Fig. d). C 3-40 hydrocarbons were produced without undesired C 1 and C 2 , as expected for bifunctional hydrocracking (Fig. e). As T carb increases, the selectivity towards C 4 -C 5 reduces, i.e., the ideality of hydrocracking increases with more “metallic” sites relative to BAS (Fig. f). Fig. g shows that W x C is tolerant to at least 10 wt% PVC. The rate increase with PVC addition is caused by the enhancement of BAS with HCl adsorption from PVC. Bimodal distribution of large PP and small oligomers without intermediates was observed from GPC (Fig. h), suggesting the sequential cleavage of each PP chain. Coke was detected on the catalysts by TGA, but completely removed to regenerate the activity with a simple H 2 treatment (Fig. i). Compared to conventional hydrocracking catalyst, W x C/SiO₂-590 shows significantly higher activity per acid site, highlighting its high efficiency.

topic: Reverse Microemulsion Synthesis As an Efficient Method for Synthesis of Highly Active Catalytic Nanomaterials for CO 2 Conversion to Renewable Synthetic Fuels
title: Reverse Microemulsion Synthesis As an Efficient Method for Synthesis of Highly Active Catalytic Nanomaterials for CO 2 Conversion to Renewable Synthetic Fuels
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: In a reverse microemulsion (RME), water nano-droplets are surrounded by surfactant molecules and dispersed in a continuous oil phase. RMEs are clear, thermodynamically stable isotropic mixtures that form by self-assembly upon mixing. Water nanodroplets can contain reactants. If two (or more) RMEs containing different reactants are mixed, the reaction happens when nanodroplets collide and merge, resulting in a gradual process of nanoparticles self-assembly. The nanoparticles are extracted by changing the RME composition, disrupting the thermodynamic stability. Upon segregation of aqueous and organic phases, nanoparticles undergo aggregation within the aqueous phase, followed by sedimentation. Various catalytic nanomaterials were synthesized using Al 2 O 3 and CeO 2 as supports and Cu, Fe, Co, Ni and Mo as active phases (as metal oxide or carbide). Resulted SSAs ranged from 200-400 m 2 /g and the nanoparticle size was less than 20 nm. The catalysts were characterized by ICP-OES, XPS, XRD, BET, and TEM to investigate chemical composition, crystallinity, and morphology. TPR and TPD were employed to investigate reducibility and adsorption properties, and in situ FTIR was used to investigate the surface reactivity. Reaction tests were conducted in a continuous flow reactor in a wide range of operating conditions such as temperature, pressure and flow rate. The outlet from the reactor was analyzed via IR and FTIR and GC. The catalysts exhibited different levels of catalytic activity and selectivity, ranging from CO and CH 4 to light hydrocarbons as products. For certain materials, CO 2 conversions approached the chemical equilibrium level (e.g., 95% CO 2 conversion and 100% selectivity). Catalyst stability was also investigated comprehensively. The results of catalytic perfomance evaluation were correlated with the results of materials characterization, while focusing on the structure-property relationship. Our work provides an avenue for developing highly efficient materials for CO 2 conversion to renewable fuels, while also providing fundamental insights into the structure-activity relationship.

topic: Batch to Continuous HTL: The Role of Temperature Profiles, Phase Heating, and Slurry Velocity in Biocrude and Char Formation
title: Batch to Continuous HTL: The Role of Temperature Profiles, Phase Heating, and Slurry Velocity in Biocrude and Char Formation
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: In Hydrothermal Liquefaction (HTL), analysis of temperature profiles is important for the optimization of the process, which typically means maximizing the amount of carbon-rich biocrude that forms while minimizing unwanted char formation. Extensive work has been done in batch HTL on this topic, however, with the limited available on these continuous-flow tests, comprehensive analysis of these temperature profiles has not been accomplished. To understand the effects of changing temperature profiles, a case study was conducted on this topic which compared batch HTL temperature profiles to continuous ones. Temperature profiles as well as mixing conditions were altered to simulate the batch conditions more closely in the continuous system. To accomplish this, different components such as a preheater and a CSTR were incorporated into the system allowing for the feed to experience different temperature gradients. This analysis revealed strong connections between heating rates and reaction temperature and the product yields and will be crucial as the design process for continuous HTL reactors continues. The effects of flowrate were also studied in the continuous system. A strong link was found between having lower flowrates and higher char yield. This connection was attributed to suspension stability where solid particulates fell out of the slurry causing more time to be spent at lower temperature ranges where repolymerization to char is more likely to occur.

topic: Controlling Metal Nanoparticle Size on Carbon Supports with Surface Tension
title: Controlling Metal Nanoparticle Size on Carbon Supports with Surface Tension
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Strong Electrostatic Adsorption (SEA) has been used for numerous metals and common oxide and carbon catalyst supports, to synthesize ultrasmall supported metal nanoparticles. In this context, “ultrasmall” refers to sizes of 1 - 2 nm. It is believed that the lower limit of nanoparticle size is caused by the formation of nanodroplets of precursor solution as the powdered supports dried – while there is no large scale migration of the metal complexes as they are strongly attracted to the support surface, surface tension replaces electrostatic interaction as drying occurs and the small deposits of precipitated precursor dictate the ultimate, reduced particle size. To achieve yet smaller particle/cluster size, we now focus on decreasing the degree the precursor agglomeration during drying. We hypothesize that metal nanoparticle size can be controlled by increasing the hydrophilicity of the carbon supports; with lower contact angles the volume of precursor nanodroplets is expected to decrease. To test this hypothesis, Ketjen Black 300 J (KB300J) and Norit SX Ultra (Norit) carbon supports, with PZCs 10 and 8 respectively, were oxidized using varied concentrations and exposure times of nitric acid to decrease the surface hydrophilicity. SEA was employed with Tetraammineplatinum(II) nitrate or Tetraamminepalladium(II) nitrate for lower PZC supports and Chloroplatinic acid or Tetrachloropalladium(II) for unoxidized supports. X-Ray Diffraction (XRD) and Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (STEM) were employed to characterize the nanoparticle size and atomic isolation of each dried and reduced catalyst. Platinum catalysts exhibit trends of decreasing particle size with higher degrees of oxidation excluding the most oxidized carbons which exhibited higher degrees of agglomeration. Dried catalysts exhibited trends of increased atomic isolation with as successive oxidation occurred with the most oxidized carbons exhibiting near entire atomic isolation. Catalysts for both carbons using Palladium will be reported.

topic: Automated Synthesis Procedure Generation in Heterogeneous Catalysis Via Fine-Tuned Large Language Model
title: Automated Synthesis Procedure Generation in Heterogeneous Catalysis Via Fine-Tuned Large Language Model
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: The exploration of catalytic materials and their synthesis routes traditionally demands extensive iterative experimentation, substantial resource allocation, and significant time investment. To overcome these constraints, we have developed an advanced extraction and classification workflow integrating sophisticated language models and multimodal processing techniques. Initially, textual data from over 9,000 scientific articles were analyzed to identify and extract detailed catalyst attributes such as chemical composition, structural motifs, morphology, crystal structure, size, shape, and support materials. Additionally, images and their associated captions were systematically captured from these publications, enriching the dataset through advanced vision-language processing methods. Subsequently, this structured information was refined through rigorous classification, synthesis query generation, and feasibility validation, resulting in a curated dataset comprising 2,250 high-quality catalyst synthesis procedures. Leveraging this dataset, we fine-tuned a large language model using parameter-efficient adaptation, significantly enhancing its capability to accurately predict detailed catalyst synthesis methods. Performance evaluation of our fine-tuned model revealed stable and effective convergence, demonstrating substantial improvements over baseline models with a ROUGE-1 score of 0.522, a ROUGE-L score of 0.290, and a BERTScore of 0.863. These results underscore the effectiveness of integrating structured multimodal data and iterative validation methods, offering a powerful new pathway to accelerate catalyst discovery and synthesis optimization, thereby reducing research timelines and resource demands.

topic: Unraveling the Homo/Heterogeneous Catalysis Pathway of Palladium Nanocatalysts Via Single-Molecule Fluorescence Imaging of the Tsuji–Trost Reaction
title: Unraveling the Homo/Heterogeneous Catalysis Pathway of Palladium Nanocatalysts Via Single-Molecule Fluorescence Imaging of the Tsuji–Trost Reaction
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Compared with the palladium molecular catalysts, the heterogeneous Pd nanocatalysts have recently increased attention and gained popularity as they potentially decrease catalyst cost, favor purification of final product, and are easily recycled. However, the mechanistic understanding of the catalytic mechanisms of palladium nanoparticle catalysts are still missing, which is partly attributed to the average signals of heterogeneous catalysts and catalytic information from most of current characterization techniques and loss of the sub-population information. Whether the reactions take place at Pd metal surface, defect edge sites of Pd nanoparticles, and/or redeposited nanoclusters through a heterogeneous pathway or leaching Pd species through a homogeneous pathway is still under debate. To resolve these issues, we employ single-molecule fluorescence techniques, total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy (TIRFM), to investigate in situ catalytic behavior of individual palladium (Pd) nanoparticles for a fluorogenic Tsuji–Trost reaction. We synthesized nanoparticles with varied sizes and shapes and evaluated their catalytic performance by tracking the formation of single product molecules on individual nanoparticles. Our findings reveal that catalysis occurs via a heterogeneous rather than homogeneous pathway. Furthermore, a direct comparison between the single-turnover rate on particles with varied shapes shows distinct differences in reactivity, potentially attributed to facet-specific effects. The imaging approach could be extended to study other types of catalytic reactions, highlighting the power of single-molecule methods for uncovering mechanistic detail at the nanocatalysts.

topic: Establishing Reaction Kinetics for LiAlH 4 Vapor Hydrolysis
title: Establishing Reaction Kinetics for LiAlH 4 Vapor Hydrolysis
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Complex Metal hydrides such as alanates (NaAlH 4 , KAlH 4 , LiAlH 4 ) and borohydrides (NaBH 4 , LiBH 4 , KBH 4 ) have gained interest among researchers due to their high gravimetric and volumetric energy densit ies, demonstrating the potential of meeting the o n-board hydrogen energy targets set by the U.S. Department of Energy. To further increase their hydrogen production potential, a lanates and b orohydrides can also undergo hydrolysis , effectively compounding the production with gas phase water splitting . While the liquid phase hydrolysis of alanates is well -studied for most alanates , the low-temperature gas-solid hydrolysis of LiAlH 4 remain s relatively unexplored and presents a unique challenge with the convolution of several kinetic steps and phase transition . This research is focused on vapor hydrolysis of LiAlH 4 in a Zero Length Column (ZLC) reactor to investigate the reaction kinetics and the influence of water vapor exposure on the efficiency of hydrogen release kinetics. The results demonstrate stoichiometric water consumption and hydrogen release that aligns with the reaction 2LiAlH 4 + 10H 2 O -> 8H 2 + LiAl 2 (OH) 6 .OH.2H 2 O + LiOH, showing that the evolved hydrogen comes from liberating both the framework and water-bound hydrogen. The rate expression is not an elementary rate order but rather expressed dependence on both solid and vapor reactants, r = k.m α LiAlH4 .P β H2O where α = 1 and β =0.57 with rate constant and activation energy of 0.0963 mol.s.kg -1.57 .m -2 and 24.7 kJ/mol respectively. The mechanism evaluation is supported by ex situ XRD, XPS and in situ DRIFTS and Raman spectroscopy that reveal the dominance of the double layered hydroxide hydration product. This study aims to provide insight that can help to optimize reaction conditions for maximum hydrogen yield.

topic: Carbonization of Low-Density Polyethylene Waste Films Using Non-Thermal Plasma
title: Carbonization of Low-Density Polyethylene Waste Films Using Non-Thermal Plasma
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: The increase in global plastic production and waste accumulation has intensified the need for more effective recycling methods. Current recycling approaches, however, pose many significant limitations, including large energy consumption and products with low quality and compromised physical properties and durability. This study aims to address both of these issues by utilizing high-voltage non-thermal plasma to upcycle plastic waste. Low-density polyethylene (LDPE) films were selected as the feedstock, and the samples were placed in a custom-made microreactor pressurized with argon gas, where high-voltage argon plasma was directly applied to the sample through the tungsten electrodes for time intervals under 15 min, ultimately carbonizing the film and simultaneously producing hydrogen gas. It was found in our study that higher applied voltage resulted in increased hydrogen production and larger carbon fraction in the solid residue (Fig. 1a). The process was able to extract approximately 40% of the hydrogen atoms from the LDPE films, leading to a yield of more than 30 mmol/gLDPE and a hydrogen production efficiency of approximately 0.1 mol/kWh (Fig. 1b). It was also observed that the major carbon-containing gas-phase product was acetylene (Fig. 1c), suggesting sooting reactions on the surface. Our experiments provided promising results and highlighted the effectiveness of using non-thermal plasma for plastic waste treatment to obtain high-value products.

topic: Catalytic Role of Noble Metals in Hydrothermal Carbonization of Loblolly Pine for Enhanced CO₂ Capture
title: Catalytic Role of Noble Metals in Hydrothermal Carbonization of Loblolly Pine for Enhanced CO₂ Capture
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: In recent years, the development of efficient and sustainable adsorbents for CO₂ capture is critical for addressing climate change. This study aims to investigate the catalytic role of noble metals in hydrothermal carbonization (HTC) of loblolly pine (LP) to enhance biomass conversion efficiency and modify hydrochar properties by introducing metal oxide functionalities and microporosity to improve its CO₂ adsorption performance. The research work aims to perform HTC experiments of LP at different temperatures varying from 200°C to 260°C using 2 wt.% of Pd, Pt, and Ni, enabling a comparative analysis of their influence on hydrochar yield, chemical composition, and physical properties. Based on performance metrics, the optimal HTC conditions (260°C with Pd) were further examined by synthesizing hydrochars with 1 wt.% and 5 wt.% Pd. The produced hydrochars after HTC at 260°C with Pd in three different wt.% were marked as metal hydrochar composites (MHCs) and further superactivated using KOH in a ratio of 2:1 at 800°C to synthesize ultraporous activated char. The MHCs were evaluated for their elemental composition, surface functionalities, thermogravimetric behavior, BET surface area, and scanning electron microscopy morphology to assess the catalytic influence of Pd at varying concentrations. Pd incorporation during HTC enhanced carbonization efficiency and introduced oxygen-containing functional groups, while post-activation significantly increased surface area and microporosity, leading to improved CO₂ adsorption capacity. Notably, CO₂ uptake increased with Pd content, with the highest adsorption capacity recorded at 5.96 mmol/g for the H260 5% Pd T8 sample. The superior CO₂ capture performance is attributed to increased surface porosity, which facilitated enhanced physical adsorption mechanisms. This study highlights the potential of Pd-assisted HTC and activation strategies in developing high-performance carbon-based adsorbents for CO₂ capture applications.

topic: Understanding the Impact of Shelf Storage on Ni–Mo Catalysts for Alkaline Hydrogen Evolution
title: Understanding the Impact of Shelf Storage on Ni–Mo Catalysts for Alkaline Hydrogen Evolution
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Hydrogen demand reached approximately 100 million tons in 2024, with over 95% produced via carbon-intensive processes like steam methane reforming. Green hydrogen, generated through water electrolysis powered by renewable energy, presents a sustainable alternative but further scaling is limited in part by the reliance on scarce and costly platinum group metals (PGMs) as catalysts. This has driven the search for cost-effective, sustainable non-PGM catalysts. Among them, nanoparticulate nickel–molybdenum (Ni–Mo) composites show promise for alkaline hydrogen chemistry, narrowing the performance gap with PGMs. This poster presents our recent findings on “shelf-life” stability of 50 wt% carbon-supported Ni-Mo composites when stored in ambient aerobic environments. Prolonged exposure to atmospheric oxygen, alters surface morphology and chemical composition; leading to a monotonic, exponential decay in HER activity with a half-life of ~1 week, as characterized by thin-film rotating disk electrode voltammetry . This loss attributed to the formation and growth of oxide layers over the metallic active sites of the nanoparticles. Catalyst samples were also examined using powder X-ray diffraction and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy. We observed a distinct increase in the intensity of features associated with oxidation over time but signals attributable to metallic Ni were still evident even after months of shelf storage. Transmission electron microscopy revealed major changes in the morphology of the catalyst, which can be summarized as disintegration of the nanoparticulate structure. Temperature programmed oxidation was performed over a range of temperatures on fresh Ni-Mo/C composites; the results indicate that catalyst oxidation proceeds in at least two distinct stages that may be consistent with an initial, fast surface reaction followed by continued oxidation under diffusion control. These experiments yield important insights about the basic physics of non-PGM catalyst degradation that is relevant to the development of ink formulation and coating strategies that diverge from methods widely used for oxidatively robust PGMs.

topic: Standard-Free Quantification of Lignin Monomers Using GC with Dual Quantitative Carbon Detection and Mass Spectrometry
title: Standard-Free Quantification of Lignin Monomers Using GC with Dual Quantitative Carbon Detection and Mass Spectrometry
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Lignin depolymerization generates a complex mixture of oxygenated monomeric compounds, posing significant challenges for quantitative analysis using traditional Gas Chromatography–Flame Ionization Detection (GC-FID) and Effective Carbon Number (ECN) methods. These conventional approaches often suffer from variable detector responses due to the presence of heteroatoms and lack the ability to quantify unknown compounds. In this study, we demonstrate the application of Gas Chromatography with Quantitative Carbon Detection and FID (GC-QCD/FID), utilizing the Polyarc™ reactor, for the quantification of lignin-derived monomers produced from Organosolv Poplar Lignin (OPL) and poplar biomass via hydrogenolysis, solvolysis, and reductive catalytic fractionation (RCF). The QCD reactor converts all organic compounds to methane prior to detection, enabling a uniform carbon response across structurally diverse products. This approach provides accurate, consistent carbon yield measurements for both known and unidentified monomeric products, offering a robust analytical tool for evaluating lignin depolymerization processes.

topic: Unveiling the Morphology–Reactivity Relationships in Metal Oxides for Catalyst Design
title: Unveiling the Morphology–Reactivity Relationships in Metal Oxides for Catalyst Design
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Heterogeneous catalysis involves the transient adsorption of reactants on the catalyst surface, rearrangement of chemical bonds, and desorption of products. Throughout these steps, the surface properties markedly govern interactions between the catalyst surface and sorbate molecules (i.e., reactants, intermediates, and products), ultimately impacting catalytic activity and selectivity. Metal oxides are an important group of heterogeneous catalysts, mainly functioning for oxidation and dehydrogenation reactions. Due to their crystalline nature, metal oxides consist of the periodic arrangement of cations and anions, and their surface structure can be significantly altered by the crystallographic cutting direction. Consequently, the exposed planes exhibit distinct electronic properties (e.g., surface charge) and geometric properties (e.g., atomic arrangement, coordination structure, interatomic distance, and defects) depending on the terminating facets. This understanding highlights the potential of shaping crystal morphology as an effective method for tuning catalytic properties. In this presentation, we will describe our studies focused on better understanding how morphology influences the surface and catalytic properties through exemplary metal oxides and catalytic reactions for the purpose of establishing more robust structure-performance relationships.

topic: Aryl-Bridged Polysesquioxane As a Support for Palladium-Catalyzed Selective Hydrogenolysis of Acetophenone: Valorizing Byproducts from Propylene Oxide Synthesis
title: Aryl-Bridged Polysesquioxane As a Support for Palladium-Catalyzed Selective Hydrogenolysis of Acetophenone: Valorizing Byproducts from Propylene Oxide Synthesis
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Propylene oxide (PO) is an essential feedstock for producing various industrial chemicals. Although several synthesis routes exist, the predominant method is the ethylbenzene co-oxidation process (PO/SM), which simultaneously produces PO and styrene monomers (SM). A major drawback of the PO/SM process is the formation of acetophenone (AP) as the main byproduct, which undermines feedstock utilization. To address this issue, AP is typically subjected to catalytic hydrogenation to yield α-methylbenzyl alcohol (α-MBA) and ethylbenzene (EB), which can be recycled back for PO synthesis process. However, this method suffers from the formation of undesired over-hydrogenated products. In this study, palladium catalysts supported on Aryl-bridged polysilsesquioxanes (ABPS), an organic–inorganic hybrid silica, were developed for enhanced AP conversion and EB selectivity. ABPS supports of different pore size were synthesized via sol–gel processing of bis(trimethoxysilylethyl)benzene in different solvents. The palladium catalysts were characterized using nitrogen physisorption, XPS, TEM, and NMR techniques. Hydrogenation reactions were performed in an autoclave reactor at 150°C and 50 bar H 2 pressure, and the reaction samples were analyzed using GC-MS. The nitrogen physisorption results suggested that the ABPS support synthesized using acetonitrile (ABPS-A) has a higher surface area and larger pore diameter compared to those of the ABPS support synthesized using tetrahydrofuran (ABPS-T). The increased pore size in ABPS-A resulted in increased Pd particle size, as confirmed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). The kinetic studies revealed that although both Pd/ABPS-A and Pd/ABPS-T catalysts achieved almost complete conversion within the first 15 min of the reaction, the Pd/ABPS-T catalyst (with smaller Pd size) was more selective for ethylbenzene, an HDO product, than Pd/ABPS-A. These results demonstrate the efficiency of our catalysts for hydrodeoxygenation without ring hydrogenation and highlight the impact of palladium particle size on HDO activity. Consequently, our Pd/ABPS catalysts emerge as promising candidates for selective catalytic hydrogenolysis of acetophenone

topic: Reaction Kinetics Analysis of Furfural Production from Xylose Dehydration and Analysis of Reactor Material Effects on Kinetic Parameters
title: Reaction Kinetics Analysis of Furfural Production from Xylose Dehydration and Analysis of Reactor Material Effects on Kinetic Parameters
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: The conversion of xylose to furfural using green solvents is a key step toward sustainable biomass valorization. In this work, furfural production was investigated in a γ-valerolactone (GVL)/water monophasic solvent system using hydrochloric acid as a homogeneous catalyst. While this system provides a promising route for high-yield furfural synthesis, our findings demonstrate that the material of the reactor plays a critical role in determining reaction performance due to metal ion leaching. Controlled batch reactions were conducted using glass reactors with added powders of industrial alloys—Hastelloy, Inconel, and stainless steel—to simulate corrosion and investigate the catalytic role of leached metal ions. Inductively coupled plasma (ICP) analysis confirmed significant ion release, particularly Fe, Cr, Ni, and Mo, depending on alloy type. These metal ions were found to influence key steps in the reaction mechanism, likely by catalyzing the isomerization of xylose to xylulose and lyxose, and affecting furfural degradation pathways. A kinetic model was developed to quantify the influence of each alloy on the rate constants of xylose conversion and furfural formation and degradation. The presence of alloy-derived ions significantly altered apparent activation energies and furfural yields. This study highlights the overlooked yet critical influence of reactor material on acid-catalyzed biomass conversion systems and offers kinetic insight essential for the optimization of scalable furfural production processes.

topic: Selective Hydrogenation with Ternary Intermetallic Catalysts
title: Selective Hydrogenation with Ternary Intermetallic Catalysts
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Binary intermetallic compounds are known to improve selectivity in partial hydrogenation by tuning active site geometry and electronic structure. Extending this concept, we explore ternary Pd-based intermetallic systems—Pd-Zn-M (M = Cu, Ag, Au), Pd-In-M (M = Cu, Ag), and Pd-Sb-M (M = Au)—which offer additional control over catalytic behavior through structural and electronic modifications. Using an integrated approach combining high-throughput design, density functional theory, microkinetic modeling, and experimental validation, we demonstrate that incorporating a third element enables fine-tuning of hydrogenation activity and selectivity. For example, adding Au to PdSb₂ alters the nanoparticle’s shape by suppressing the (111) facet and favoring the (100) surface. Although Au is not directly involved at the active site, it modulates which surface facets are exposed, which in turn affects the catalytic pathway. This prediction is supported by surface energy calculations and validated by electron backscatter diffraction. Experimental reactivity measurements and modeling show that changes in facet exposure influence surface coverage and reaction energetics, thereby impacting the semi-hydrogenation of acetylene. Microkinetic simulations confirm that the modified surface structure leads to improved selectivity by altering key intermediates and pathways. Ternary intermetallics expand the design space for catalyst development, enabling precise control of active site structure and reactivity. The computationally-guided approach demonstrates a powerful strategy for rationally designing selective hydrogenation catalysts.

topic: Elucidation of Solvent Effects: Comparing Gas and Condensed Phase CO 2 Hydrogenation
title: Elucidation of Solvent Effects: Comparing Gas and Condensed Phase CO 2 Hydrogenation
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Integrated carbon capture and conversion (ICCC) has been put forward as a promising technique, among many, for the mitigation of atmospheric CO 2 . Heterogeneous catalysis has been proposed as the means of converting captured form CO 2 (typically a carbamate or carbonate) to valorized products such as methanol via reactive separation. A key issue in the development of this technology is the harsh conditions brought on by capture agent mediated reactions, and lack of harmony between capture agent solvent and catalyst. A large white space exists in the literature regarding solvent effects relevant to condensed phase CO 2 hydrogenation. The current paradigm of condensed phase catalyst design is to simply use a successful gas phase catalyst in a solvent, with little regard to the stability of either the solvent or catalyst. To address this, an industrially used methanol catalyst, Cu/ZnO/Al 2 O 3 , reacted with CO 2 and H 2 in a high pressure packed bed reactor and in a batch reactor to directly compare the gas and condensed phase at identical reaction temperature, reaction pressure, catalyst loading, and reagent ratio. Cyclohexane, Hexane, Acetone, Water, Toluene and Ethanol were used as solvents to encompass a wide array of solvent parameters. Effects of dielectric constant, Kamlett and Taft parameters and molecular diameters on catalyst stability and activity are explored. Further, the impact of solvent choice on reaction mechanism is elucidated via the use of 13 C enriched CO 2 and in-situ magic angle spinning NMR.

topic: Structure Property Relationship of Pt Cluster Catalysts for Propane Dehydrogenation
title: Structure Property Relationship of Pt Cluster Catalysts for Propane Dehydrogenation
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Pt subnanometer cluster catalysts with promoting metals and tuned particle sizes have been synthesized on various supports to improve the selectivity and stability for propane (C 3 H 8 ) dehydrogenation (PDH) to propylene (C 3 H 6 ). Among them, PtZn clusters supported on zeolites emerged to exhibit superior PDH performance, including high activity and selectivity, and good stability. Considering the tremendous interest in atomically dispersed and sub-nanometer metallic catalysts, our work aims to develop their structure-property relationships. Here, the roles of Pt nuclearity and promoter Zn, on activity and selectivity are elucidated, based on the investigation of PDH mechanism on Pt x Zn y (x=1-3, y=0-3) clusters on Silicalite-1 zeolite using density functional theory (DFT) calculations, microkinetic modeling (MKM), and experimental measurements. We find that the coordination of a Pt atom to a nest of grafted Zn atoms increases the stability of the Pt 1 Zn y sites, whose activity is similar for y=0–2 and drops dramatically for y>2. We further demonstrate, via linear scaling relations and MKM, that the turnover frequency obeys a volcano law as a function of propylene binding strength (Figure 1). The Pt 2 Zn 1 and Pt 3 Zn 1 sites are stable and exhibit activity similar to Pt 1 Zn 2 , but only Pt 1 Zn 2 manifests reaction kinetics consistent with experimental data, strongly suggesting the active site composition in the synthesized catalyst samples. The methodology presented here also suggests a general strategy for deducing active site information such as composition through simple kinetic experiments. In addition, propylene binding strength has been found as a universal descriptor for propane dehydrogenation activity and is used to predict activity for other Pt cluster catalysts.

However, C-C linkages are the most resistant in the molecule, so even though the disassembly process chosen to break the linkages could not be enough to break them. Moreover, most of the research approaches on lignin depolymerization under multiple methods and catalysis applied have mostly produced phenols, but the production of valuable ketones and aromatic acids requires multiple steps and downstream processes that increases the complexity of the synthesis. Previously it was able to coordinated three manganese species [Mn(II), Mn(0) and Mn(III)] with Ethylammonium formate (EAF) to achieve a catalyst framework which completed fast dehydrogenation breaking C-C and C-O bonds presented on the structure 1,4 dimethoxybenzene. The study of the catalyst on Kraft lignin depolymerization is the key to analyze the activity of these three catalysts and results in bond breakage and targeted valuable products such as Ketones and aromatics using characterization techniques such as GC-MS. Finally, with the purpose of applying this project to real life, it is looking for a scaling up process that will apply engineering considerations such as reactor design, heat transfer and mixing for a future commercialization of the catalyst. topic: Dry Reforming (CO2) of Higher Hydrocarbons for Green Hydrogen Production
title: Dry Reforming (CO2) of Higher Hydrocarbons for Green Hydrogen Production
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: The increasing global demand for sustainable energy and the need for effective utilization of greenhouse gases have intensified research into dry reforming processes (Utilization of CO 2 as a feed). Dry reforming of propane and higher hydrocarbons (C3+) produces synthesis gas (syngas) which is a mixture of hydrogen (H2) and carbon monoxide (CO) using carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) as a reactant. The process offers dual benefits: the conversion of light and heavy hydrocarbons into valuable syngas, and the reduction of CO 2 emissions through utilization. The study focuses on the thermodynamic, kinetic, and catalytic aspects of the dry reforming process. Rhenium-based catalysts, enhanced with promoters and supported on metal oxides, are evaluated due to their cost-effectiveness and activity. However, challenges such as catalyst deactivation due to carbon deposition (coking) and sintering are analyzed. The effect of reaction temperature, pressure, and CO 2 to hydrocarbon molar ratio on product distribution is systematically explored, with a particular emphasis on optimizing H 2 /CO ratios for downstream applications like Fischer-Tropsch synthesis and hydrogen production. The findings contribute to advancing sustainable industrial processes by efficiently transforming hydrocarbons and CO 2 into valuable energy resources while reducing environmental impact. This research provides insights into the potential of dry reforming as a viable technology for energy production and CO 2 mitigation, paving the way for future developments in low-carbon fuel generation and green chemistry applications.

topic: Supercritical Hydrothermal Liquefaction of Waste Woody Biomass
title: Supercritical Hydrothermal Liquefaction of Waste Woody Biomass
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: This study aims to improve the quality of biocrude produced from the hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) of waste woody biomass and enhance its potential as a feedstock for making sustainable aviation fuel. HTL is conducted at temperatures of 375 °C and pressures exceeding 3400 psi to depolymerize woody biomass under supercritical water conditions. HTL reactions are performed in both batch and continuous modes to examine the effect of heating and cooling rates on the depolymerization of woody biomass. A particle residence time of 15 minutes is selected for the batch HTL reactions once the desired temperature is reached. The same residence time is applied for the continuous HTL reactor. Additionally, we compare how varying process parameters, such as the reactor's initial pressure, influence the yield, composition, and quality of the biocrude produced. The HTL liquor is separated from the char via filtration. The liquor then undergoes solvent extraction to separate the organic phase from the aqueous phase. Ethyl acetate is used as the solvent due to its low solubility in water and relatively low boiling point compared to water. Various analytical techniques are employed to determine the components of the biocrude. Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) Spectroscopy is used to identify functional groups, while conventional gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and comprehensive two-dimensional gas chromatography (GC×GC) are used to analyze the composition of the biocrude and the aqueous phase. GC×GC offers advantages over conventional GC-MS due to its ability to resolve complex mixtures and distinguish compounds with similar boiling points. The GC-MS analysis showed that the HTL oil contained phenols, benzenediols, cycloketones , and ethers . Although these oxygenated molecules increase the biocrude's energy density, they also make it more unstable and chemically reactive , indicating the need for further upgrading.

topic: Co-Hydrothermal Liquefaction of Organosolv and Alkaline Lignin: Statistical Evaluation of Process Parameter Effects on Biocrude and Solid Char
title: Co-Hydrothermal Liquefaction of Organosolv and Alkaline Lignin: Statistical Evaluation of Process Parameter Effects on Biocrude and Solid Char
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Lignin, a complex and heterogeneous biopolymer, varies in structure depending on its extraction method, influencing its reactivity during hydrothermal liquefaction. Organosolv lignin resembles native lignin, retaining a higher proportion of ether linkages and minimal impurities. In contrast, alkaline lignin undergoes structural modifications that reduce ether linkages and introduce alkaline functional groups in its structure, making it more water-soluble. Literature indicates that alkaline catalysts enhance lignin depolymerization, improving biocrude yields. Thus, the coliquefaction of organosolv and alkaline lignin might work as a promising pathway, potentially improving conversion efficiency and product quality. This study investigates the co-hydrothermal liquefaction(co-HTL) of alkaline and organosolv lignin to assess the impact of reaction conditions on product yield and energy content. An L9 Taguchi design was used to systematically examine the effects of reaction temperature (270-310°C), AL fraction (15-45 wt%), and residence time (15-45 min). The results were further analyzed using ANOVA to determine the statistical significance of the effect. Results indicate that biocrude yield ranged from 9.2 ± 0.2 to 14.1 ± 0.1 wt%, with no statistically significant influence from any individual process parameter indicating the interaction effect. However, its energy content increased with temperature and AL fraction, shifting toward a more energy-dense biocrude. Solid char yield varied from 53.2 ± 0.8 to 67.0 ± 0.6 wt%, decreasing with an increase in temperature, while residence time had no significant effect. In contrast to biocrude, the energy content of solid char remained statistically unchanged across all conditions. These findings provide statistical clarification on the role of key process variables in co-HTL, offering insights into optimizing lignin-derived biofuels for improved energy applications.

topic: Desulfurization of 2-Phenylcyclohexanethiol over CoP and Co 2 p
title: Desulfurization of 2-Phenylcyclohexanethiol over CoP and Co 2 p
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Driven by the growing demand for ultraclean fuels, deep HDS has received great attention. To achieve deep HDS, the most refractory sulfurcontaining compounds, dibenzothiophene (DBT) and its alkylated derivatives (DBTs), must be removed from transportation fuels. Hence, an in-depth understanding of the HDS mechanisms of these molecules is prerequisite for the development of efficient HDS catalysts. There are three types of C–S bonds (the aryl C–S bond, the vinyl C–S bond, and the cycloalkyl C–S bond) in the HDS networks of DBT and DBTs. The cleavage of the aryl and vinyl C–S bonds occurs mainly through hydrogenolysis, while in the initial cycloalkyl C–S bond-breaking was a challenge to confirm b-elimination and hydrogenolysis due to the b-elimination products are further hydrogenated under H 2 . In addition, hydrogen is a reactant in hydrogenolysis, but is not required for b-elimination. We studied the desulfurization of 2-phenylcyclohexanethiol (2-PCHT) over CoP, and Co 2 P under H 2 or Ar. 2-PCHT, a chemically reasonable intermediate in the HDS of DBT, is similar to that of HH-DBT, but only possesses a cycloalkyl C–S bond, is an ideal model compound to get an in-depth understanding of the cleavage of the cycloalkyl C–S bond and the catalytic properties of transition-metal phosphides. The hydrodesulfurization of 2-PCHT proceeded through three parallel pathways: b-elimination, hydrogenolysis, and dehydrogenation. Under Ar, the parallel pathways were b-elimination, hydrogenolysis or homolytic C-S bond cleavage, and dehydrogenation. CoP was more active than Co 2 P under H 2 , while they were almost equal under Ar. b-Elimination dominated the desulfurization of 2-PCHT over CoP and Co 2 P, while Under Ar, dehydrogenation pathways increases under Ar compared with that under H 2 . The inhibiting effects of piperidine depended on the reaction and catalyst. Phosphosulfide phases were formed under both H 2 and Ar, but the sulfidation behavior of CoP was different from that of Co 2 P.

topic: Stabilizing Calcium Nitride for Efficient Ammonia Synthesis
title: Stabilizing Calcium Nitride for Efficient Ammonia Synthesis

abstract: Calcium-mediated electrochemical ammonia synthesis presents a sustainable alternative to the Haber–Bosch process, though its advancement is limited by gas–liquid mass transport inefficiencies, slow hydrogen oxidation kinetics, and solvent degradation. In this work, we address these challenges by (i) implementing high-activity anodes to enhance hydrogen oxidation and suppress solvent breakdown, (ii) replacing tetrahydrofuran (THF) with a more chemically stable ether-based solvent, dimethoxyethane (DME), and (iii) designing a custom polyetheretherketone (PEEK) flow cell to improve gas–liquid interfacial stability. These system-level improvements support stable calcium nitride formation, confirmed by in-situ Raman and post-electrolysis XPS, and highlight the role of interfacial engineering in maintaining reactivity and selectivity. Isotope-labeling with ¹⁵N₂ confirms N₂ as the nitrogen source, and kinetic studies reveal the influence of anode material on hydrogen oxidation and overall cell performance. This work establishes critical mechanistic understanding and design principles for reliable and efficient calcium-mediated nitrogen fixation under continuous operation.

topic: Sustainable Upcycling of Urea and Methane from Waste Stream through Zeolite-enzyme Tandem Catalysis
title: Sustainable Upcycling of Urea and Methane from Waste Stream through Zeolite-enzyme Tandem Catalysis

abstract: Urea (CO(NH₂)₂) plays a central role in our synthetic methanotrophic system, in which two catalysts—Fe-ZSM-5 and alcohol oxidase—convert methane into formaldehyde, which subsequently reacts with urea to form urea-formaldehyde polymers. The addition of urea not only facilitates polymer formation but also prevents the over-oxidation of carbon intermediates. In terms of mass balance, urea accounts for approximately two-thirds of the final polymer’s mass. Industrially, urea is synthesized by reacting ammonia with carbon dioxide under high-temperature, high-pressure conditions. The primary source of ammonia is the energy-intensive Haber–Bosch process, which contributes over 2% of global energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions, with 42% of produced ammonia used for urea synthesis. These limitations underscore the need for more sustainable methods of urea production under ambient conditions. While urea can be synthesized via catalytic co-reduction of nitrogen and carbon dioxide, it is also abundantly available as a waste product—particularly in human urine, which contains approximately 200–300 mM urea. Although technologies such as adsorption, membrane separation, and hydrolysis have been proposed for urea removal, there is currently no widely adopted method for recovering urea as a chemical feedstock. In this study, we demonstrate that urea derived from human urine can be directly utilized in our tandem catalytic system—comprising alcohol oxidase and Fe-ZSM-5—to produce methylene diurea (MDU), a key monomer in urea-formaldehyde polymerization. Urine was diluted in phosphate buffer to adjust urea concentrations and minimize interference from biomolecules, enabling efficient polymer formation with higher selectivity and productivity than systems using synthetic urea. These findings present a promising strategy for the chemical upcycling of urea from waste streams into value-added polymeric materials, offering dual benefits of nitrogen waste remediation and sustainable material production. topic: Understanding Bimetallic Interactions and Deactivation Pathways in Mo-Fe/ZSM-5 Catalysts for Methane Dehydroaromatization

abstract: Methane dehydroaromatization (MDA) offers a sustainable, greenhouse gas-free route to convert methane into value-added products like benzene and hydrogen, presenting a promising alternative to petroleum-based feedstocks. However, rapid catalyst deactivation and low yields remain key challenges. Molybdenum (Mo) supported on ZSM-5 is among the most effective monometallic catalysts, and Fe-promoted Mo/ZSM-5 systems have shown enhanced activity. Yet, the precise role of Mo-Fe interactions in improving performance remains poorly understood due to characterization challenges. In this work, we present a detailed investigation into the formation of distinct active sites in bimetallic Mo-Fe/ZSM-5 catalysts compared to their monometallic counterparts, Mo/ZSM-5 and Fe/ZSM-5. Catalysts were synthesized via co-impregnation to achieve the co-location of Mo and Fe species within the zeolite framework. Advanced characterization techniques, including XPS, UV-Vis, and Raman spectroscopy revealed the formation of unique bimetallic active sites, possibly a bimetallic carbide (MoFeCx) phase, which significantly enhanced methane conversion and benzene selectivity. At equivalent methane conversion, the Mo-Fe/ZSM-5 catalyst exhibited up to 150% higher benzene formation rate compared to Mo/ZSM-5. Characterization of spent catalysts also indicates that polyaromatic coke, rather than graphitic coke on the zeolite surface, is the primary cause of catalyst deactivation. The bimetallic Mo-Fe/ZSM-5 catalyst effectively suppresses aromatic coke formation and promotes the growth of carbon nanotubes, resulting in a lower deactivation rate compared to Mo/ZSM-5. Consequently, the bimetallic catalyst exhibits superior activity and stability, demonstrating its potential for enhanced performance in methane aromatization. This study bridges a key knowledge gap by elucidating the structural and functional effects of Mo-Fe interactions, offering a foundation for designing more efficient and stable catalysts to advance methane valorization technologies and other reactions (i.e., selective reduction of NOx, biomass conversion, methanol aromatization (MTA), etc.) where these are the catalysts of choice.

topic: Conversion of Carbon Dioxide to Value-Added Products
title: Conversion of Carbon Dioxide to Value-Added Products
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: The escalating levels of carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions, driven by population growth and industrialization, pose a critical challenge to global climate stability. In response, advanced technologies in Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) are emerging as transformative tools in the transition to a carbon-neutral economy. This paper explores a comprehensive suite of chemical and bio-integrated strategies for CO₂ conversion, spanning catalytic, electrochemical, and nanomaterial-based methods. Catalytic conversion techniques—such as dry reforming of methane and plasma-based CO₂ splitting—are complemented by innovative catalysts including doped carbon materials, single-atom catalysts, and polyoxometalates. Electrochemical reduction and hybrid systems like artificial photosynthesis integrate renewable energy into carbon valorization. Bio-CCU pathways leverage microalgae and engineered microbes to offer energy-efficient carbon conversion and sequestration. Additionally, nanostructured materials like MOFs, COFs, and carbon nanotubes are being explored for scalable electroreduction and hydrogen production. This multidisciplinary approach underscores the need for integrated systems combining chemistry, materials science, and biotechnology to sustainably reduce atmospheric CO₂ and generate valuable products and fuels. The study highlights the critical role of innovation, scalability, and policy in deploying these technologies toward a circular, low-carbon future.

topic: Kinetics of Heavy Reformate Transalkylation over a ZSM-5-Mordenite Catalyst
title: Kinetics of Heavy Reformate Transalkylation over a ZSM-5-Mordenite Catalyst
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Reformate is the major source of bulk aromatic chemicals in refineries, including benzene, toluene, and xylene. To maximize the production of these chemicals, heavy reformate is processed in transalkylation units where predominantly trimethylbenzenes are reacted with toluene to give xylenes. In this work, the kinetics of heavy reformate transalkylation in the presence of toluene and H 2 at 598-648 K and 2.0 MPa was studied over a proprietary ZSM-5-mordenite catalyst. A kinetic model was developed based on dealkylation, transalkylation, and disproportionation reactions. The dealkylation of alkylbenzenes, namely propylbenzene, methylethylbenzene, and methylpropylbenzene, was found to exhibit the highest rates among the reactions considered, resulting in the formation of benzene and toluene. The transalkylation of trimethylbenzenes with toluene and the disproportionation of toluene were found to proceed at similar activation barriers (56-57 kJ mol -1 ), giving rise to the formation of benzene and xylenes. Measured rates signify the transalkylation of trimethylbenzenes with toluene as a prevalent pathway to mixed xylenes. Figure 1 . topic: Stability of Lactate Esters and Their Zeolite-Catalyzed Conversion to Acrylates: Effects of Alcohol-Water Solvent Systems
title: Stability of Lactate Esters and Their Zeolite-Catalyzed Conversion to Acrylates: Effects of Alcohol-Water Solvent Systems
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Lactic acid and alkyl lactate esters are fermentation products of lignocellulosic biomass, currently used as food and pharmaceutical additives, monomers for compostable plastics, and green solvents. Furthermore, lactates are structurally similar to acrylic acid and can serve as renewable precursors in the synthesis of acrylates for use in paints, sealants, and polymers. In this work, we examined the stability of methyl and ethyl lactate under storage conditions and described an autocatalytic mechanism for lactate ester hydrolysis. We found that low temperature, low water content, and the presence of added alcohol all serve to slow the rate of hydrolysis to lactic acid. We then evaluated the effects of water and alcohol content on the conversion of lactates to acrylates. Feeds containing a combination of alkyl lactate with water and/or alcohol were vaporized and reacted over sodium-exchanged Faujasite-type zeolite. In addition to stabilizing the lactate feed, the addition of 5-10 mol % alcohol resulted in a 50%-140% increase in molar selectivity as compared to the solely aqueous lactate solutions. The magnitude of this selectivity improvement was dependent on the identity of the alkyl group(s) associated with the lactate ester and the alcohol. Further addition of alcohol beyond 10 mol% did not further increase selectivity. These results show the benefits of including alcohol in methyl or ethyl lactate feeds, resulting in both increased reactant stability and improved performance in the conversion of lactates to sustainable acrylates.

topic: Tandem Catalytic Hydrothermal Liquefaction of Spent Coffee Grounds Using Zeolite-Supported Metal Catalysts for Biofuel Production
title: Tandem Catalytic Hydrothermal Liquefaction of Spent Coffee Grounds Using Zeolite-Supported Metal Catalysts for Biofuel Production
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) of biomass is an emerging thermochemical conversion technique to produce biofuels. Typically, biomass HTL uses pressurized water (at 250-400°C, and 10-35 MPa). HTL offers several inherent advantages, including 1) cost-effectiveness, compared with other biomass chemical processes such as pyrolysis and gasification, and 2) feedstock flexibility by accepting various biomass types (e.g., wood, plant, biomass waste, manure, and sewage sludge). However, current biomass HTL technologies lead to biocrude oil, which is unsuitable for transportation fuels. This is because biocrude oil contains high oxygen (O) contents (10-50 wt%), compared to commercial gasoline and diesel fuels (0.0-2.2 wt%). To address this challenge, we investigated tandem catalytic HTL of biomass using biphasic solvents (i.e., water and hydrophobic solvent) with zeolite-supported catalysts, which enable oxygen-containing biocrude oil to concurrently undergo hydrodeoxygenation with H 2 to biofuels with reduced oxygen contents in hydrophobic solvents during reactions. Spent coffee grounds (SCG), which are biomass waste generated daily, have been used as biomass resources for this study. In this poster presentation, the following effects on catalytic performance for the reactions will be discussed through catalyst synthesis and characterization, and its reaction performance evaluation: 1) types of catalysts (earth abundant metals (such as Ni, Co and Cu) on zeolites), 2) types and ratios of water-hydrophobic solvents (e.g., cyclohexane and n-octane), hydrogen pressure, 3) H 2 pressure, and 4) reaction temperature and time. This research will provide insights into the feasibility of direct biofuel production from tandem catalytic SCG HTL, and will also be applicable to other types of biomass resources due to feedstock flexibility enabled by HTL.

topic: Elucidation on Hydrothermal Carbonization Reaction Using Unreacted-Core Shrinking Model
title: Elucidation on Hydrothermal Carbonization Reaction Using Unreacted-Core Shrinking Model
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Valorization of waste biomass is a topic of great interest nowadays, because it helps mitigate greenhouse gas emission, soil and water pollution etc. through the production of biofuels, fertilizers and other useful chemicals. There are different processes for this waste valorization, such as, anaerobic digestion, pyrolysis, gasification, hydrothermal carbonization (HTC) etc. Among these processes, HTC is the most suitable for handling biomass with high moisture content. HTC is a moderately high pressure high temperature process that devolatilizes the light organic compounds from the feedstock and yields a solid called hydrochar, which is more energy and nutrient dense. Understanding the underlying mechanism of HTC will allow for fine-tuned hydrochar properties for specific use and aid in reactor and process design. The goal of this study was to elucidate on the mechanism of the HTC reaction. To meet this goal, first, HTC experiments were carried out in a 25 mL reactor placed in a sand bath to get the mass loss profile with time at three different temperatures, 160 °C, 180 °C and 200 °C. Then, the unreacted-core shrinking model was used to elucidate on the mechanism of HTC of a model molecule, cellulose. Here, it was assumed that as the HTC reaction progresses, a porous product layer keeps on replacing the reacted portion of the biomass particle. The reactant water monomers must then diffuse through the product layer to reach the shrinking core surface. The model was solved numerically to estimate different physical and chemical parameters i.e., diffusion coefficient, reaction order, pre-exponential factor, stoichiometric coefficient and activation through optimization using experimental data from 160 °C and 200 °C. Then these estimated parameter values were used to predict the mass loss profile for HTC at 180 °C. The results were found to be in well agreement with experimental data with <5% error.

topic: Tuning Zeolite Synthesis for Improved Performance of Ti-Beta Zeolites in Olefin Epoxidation
title: Tuning Zeolite Synthesis for Improved Performance of Ti-Beta Zeolites in Olefin Epoxidation
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Achieving high activity and selectivity in epoxidation of olefins is challenging, but it is crucial in the refinement of production of epoxides. Further, it is desirable to develop pathways to high activity and selectivity without using an organic oxidant. Thus, zeolites are appealing candidates for catalysts for epoxidation. Specifically, it is established that Ti-Beta is an active candidate for this reaction, which can be run using hydrogen peroxide as a non-organic oxidant. As with any heterogeneous catalyst, many facets of Ti-Beta appear to influence the reaction, but our understanding of all factors is incomplete. Our goal is to establish how to establish how to increase the activity and selectivity of this important catalyst. In this study, we have used different titanium precursors during hydrothermal synthesis to identify the impact on catalyst activity and selectivity. The materials have similar structural and textural properties, but the precursor affects the active site. By testing each catalyst for epoxidation activity, this study achieves a greater understanding of the effects of material properties of Ti-Beta on catalytic activity and provides a framework for future testing and implementation.

topic: In Situ Generation of GaN Species in Zeolite CHA Cages By Scavenging Framework Gallium
title: In Situ Generation of GaN Species in Zeolite CHA Cages By Scavenging Framework Gallium
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Beyond its significance in optoelectronics and semiconductors, gallium nitride (GaN) has gained attention in the catalysis field, particularly since its discovery as a thermal catalyst for non-oxidative aromatization of alkanes. Here we investigate the in-situ generation of extra-framework GaN species within the small-pore Ga-zeolite (e.g., chabazite, CHA) via a concerted decomposition and demetallation process. This method involves nitridation through the decomposition of a nitrogen source (e.g., ammonia) with concomitant extraction of framework gallium, forming a GaN within cha cages. This approach avoids post-synthesis ion exchange, which is challenging in confined zeolite pores. GaN formation was validated through three techniques: (1) a color change from white (H-Ga-CHA) to yellow ([GaN]-Ga-CHA), intensifying with Ga content; (2) powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD), confirming parent H-Ga-CHA zeolites without impurities, with peak shifts towards lower angles due to the insertion of Ga in the framework and an evolution of GaN peak; and (3) X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), showing increased extra-framework GaN with higher GaN content. Finally, we assess the performance of [GaN]-Ga-CHA catalysts relative to the [Ga]-Ga-CHA catalysts for ethane dehydrogenation (EDH). H-Ga-CHA parent sample, containing predominantly framework Ga, exhibits low activity. On the other hand, the [Ga]-Ga-CHA samples containing a higher percentage of extra-framework Ga exhibit higher initial ethylene formation rates. The [GaN]-Ga-CHA with the highest GaN content demonstrates a similar EDH performance to that of the [Ga]-Ga-CHA. Our study highlights the proof of principle for the method of scavenging metals in zeolites frameworks to generate multifunctional catalysts in situ, thereby circumventing the difficulties associated with encapsulating large active sites in small pores of zeolite catalysts.

topic: Confining Platinum Clusters in Indium-Modified ZSM-5 Zeolite to Promote Propane Dehydrogenation
title: Confining Platinum Clusters in Indium-Modified ZSM-5 Zeolite to Promote Propane Dehydrogenation
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Designing highly active and stable catalytic sites is often challenging due to the complex synthesis procedure and the agglomeration of active sites during high-temperature reactions. Here, we report a facile two-step method to synthesize Pt clusters confined by In-modified ZSM-5 zeolite. In-situ characterization confirms that In is located at the extra-framework position of ZSM-5 as In + , and the Pt clusters are stabilized by the In-ZSM-5 zeolite. The resulting Pt clusters confined in In-ZSM-5 show excellent propane conversion, propylene selectivity, and catalytic stability, outperforming monometallic Pt, In, and bimetallic PtIn alloys. The incorporation of In + in ZSM-5 neutralizes Brønsted acid sites to inhibit side reactions, as well as tunes the electronic properties of Pt clusters to facilitate propane activation and propylene desorption. The strategy of combining precious metal clusters with metal cation-exchanged zeolites opens the avenue to develop stable heterogeneous catalysts for other reaction systems.
