topic: Reaction Pathways of Non-Oligomer Products in Olefin Oligomerization Catalyzed By Ga³⁺ Lewis Acid Sites
title: Reaction Pathways of Non-Oligomer Products in Olefin Oligomerization Catalyzed By Ga³⁺ Lewis Acid Sites
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: High metal-loading Ga/SiO 2 and Ga/Al 2 O 3 catalysts were synthesized to investigate the effect of support materials on the catalyst structures and catalytic performance for olefin oligomerization. XAS analysis revealed that Ga 3+ ions with four Ga-O bonds interact differently with SiO 2 and Al 2 O 3 supports, with two Ga-O-Si bonds on Ga/SiO 2 and four Ga-O-Al bonds on Ga/Al 2 O 3 . Pyridine IR spectra confirmed the presence of Lewis acid sites without Brønsted acid sites on both catalysts, with Ga/SiO 2 exhibiting stronger Lewis acidity. While Lewis acids are not typically known to react with hydrocarbons, under coordinated Lewis acidic Ga 3+ sites were found to catalyze oligomerization and secondary reactions including hydrogen transfer, olefins isomerization, and C-C bond fragmentation, leading to non-oligomer products. These non-oligomer products can further react at higher conversions, leading to the formation of other higher molecular weight non-oligomers. Thus, this work aims to elucidate the source of non-oligomer products from olefin oligomerization at elevated temperatures. Given that C 6 olefins are the major primary products in both ethylene and propylene oligomerization on Lewis acidic Ga/SiO 2 and Ga/Al 2 O 3 catalysts, it is hypothesized that these C 6 olefins undergo secondary reactions such as C-C bond fragmentation on Lewis acidic Ga 3+ sites. Both experimental and theoretical studies will be presented to provide insight into the C–C bond fragmentation pathway on Ga 3+ Lewis acid catalysts for olefin oligomerization.

topic: Zeolite/LDH Composites As Additives for Light Olefin Production By Catalytic Cracking of Heavy Petroleum Oils.
title: Zeolite/LDH Composites As Additives for Light Olefin Production By Catalytic Cracking of Heavy Petroleum Oils.
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Light olefins, especially propylene, are key building blocks in the petrochemical industry [1], mainly produced via steam cracking of hydrocarbons [2] or fluid catalytic cracking (FCC) of heavy feedstocks such as vacuum gas oil (VGO) [3]. The latter process presents the advantages of its ability to handle heavy oil fractions and to selectively adjust the product distributions [3c]. One of the most cost effective and efficient routes to enhance light olefins yield is the addition of catalyst additives to USY-based FCC catalysts. The medium pore zeolite ZSM-5 is one of the most studied FCC additives, producing predominantly propene and butenes [3b] but also light alkanes by undesired bimolecular hydrogen transfer reactions. Thus, the design of new additives with higher selectivity to LPG olefins is of high interest. Herein, we present an efficient additive based on a composite material derived from ZSM-5 and layered double hydroxides (Z5-LDH). The increase in LPG olefin production is attributed to the lower Brønsted acid sites and acid strength in Z5-LDH, which minimizes secondary reactions such as hydrogen transfer. Moreover, the basic metal oxide generated from the LDH material suppresses the re-adsorption of produced LPG olefins, reducing their conversion and increasing their final yield. This additive has shown benefits not only in VGO cracking but also in the conversion of other heavier feedstock such as ATM residue.

topic: Synthesis of a Robust Macroporosity-Free Mesoporous Silica Compacts
title: Synthesis of a Robust Macroporosity-Free Mesoporous Silica Compacts
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Despite the widespread interest in mesoporous materials, large-scale, mechanically robust mesoporous solids are still lacking. This is mainly due to the difficulty of maintaining mesostructural order (at the nanometer) over macroscale ranges (centimeters) using supramolecular self-assembly processes. To overcome this limitation, we developed a multi-step process, involving 1) synthesis of a mesostructured silica powder with an SBA-16 type ordered framework using typical supramolecular assembly methods, 2) consolidation of the powder into an inch-sized robust pellet using spark plasma sintering (SPS), and 3) transformation of the unwanted macroporous network formed during the consolidation process into an ordered mesoporous structure. The last step is done by repeated infiltration of the macropores with a silica solution containing structure-directing polymers, which assemble into the same SBA-16 type cubic mesostructured phase present in the original silica powder. The fabricated monoliths are highly permeable with a surface area exceeding 270 m 2 /g from a continuous SBA-16 cubic mesoporous matrix. This new type of mesoporous solids exhibits excellent mechanical stability comparable to sedimentary rocks, despite having a low density of only ~1.1 g/cm 3 .

topic: Optimization of a Colombian-Cassava-Starch-Based Starbon® Surface Properties for Its Use As Fatty Acid Esterification Catalyst
title: Optimization of a Colombian-Cassava-Starch-Based Starbon® Surface Properties for Its Use As Fatty Acid Esterification Catalyst
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Starbon® materials are mesoporous carbons obtained from polysaccharides with industrial potential in catalysis and adsorption applications. While these materials are traditionally synthesized from high-amylose starches (e.g., Hylon VII), this work explores Colombian cassava starch—a low-cost, low-amylose alternative—to produce Starbon® materials, addressing agro-industrial waste valorization while tailoring properties for fatty acid esterification (key to cosmetics and food industries). The transformation of cassava starch into functional Starbon® materials presents unique challenges, particularly in developing adequate porosity during the synthesis process, which involves gelatinization, retrogradation, and controlled carbonization. Challenges in porosity development (negligible pore volume in initial cassava-Starbon® trials) were overcome by optimizing gelatinization (mass ratio, temperature) and carbonization via factorial (3²) and Box-Behnken designs. Statistical analysis revealed mass ratio (1:12 starch:water) and 105-110°C gelatinization temperature as critical for maximizing surface area (>300 m²/g) and pore volume, while carbonization at 450°C ensured structural stability. Tukey tests confirmed these factors’ significance (p < 0.05), with optimal conditions yielding mesopores (5–50 nm), avoiding diffusional limitations for large fatty acid esters (kinetic diameters: 0.8–1.5 nm). The resulting sulfonated cassava-Starbon® demonstrated lipophilicity, high acid density (>1.5 mmol/g), and recyclability—overcoming drawbacks tipically observed when performing esterification of fatty acids using hydrophilic ion-exchange resins. This study establishes cassava starch as a viable precursor for Starbon® catalysts, with tuned porosity and surface properties to be used as catalysts for esterification of bulky substrates. The methodology aligns with Colombia’s potential of oleochemical and starch-based feedstocks, offering a sustainable pathway for the production of high-value biobased products.

topic: Selective Removal of SOx, NOx and H2S Using NiO/SBA-15 in a Chemical Looping-Based Pollutant Removal Scheme.
title: Selective Removal of SOx, NOx and H2S Using NiO/SBA-15 in a Chemical Looping-Based Pollutant Removal Scheme.
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Greenhouse gas emissions from flue gas generated during fossil fuel combustion remain a critical contributor to global climate change. While carbon capture technologies are advancing, flue gas still contains NOx, SOx, and H 2 S—pollutants that must be removed to avoid further process inefficiencies. Conventional treatment methods rely on multiple systems—flue gas desulfurization (FGD) for SOx, claus process for H 2 S, and selective catalytic reduction (SCR) for NOx—each adding cost, energy demand, and complexity due to separate units and infrastructure. We propose a novel chemical looping approach for selective removal of NO x , SO x , and H 2 S using a single-reactor system to address these limitations. This system employs nickel oxide (NiO) as the oxygen carrier due to its high reactivity and inertness towards CO 2 . Upon reduction to metallic Ni, the material undergoes cyclic redox reactions, selectively interacting with target pollutants while maintaining a pure CO 2 stream. To improve dispersion and stability, NiO was supported on mesoporous SBA-15 using a wet impregnation, forming NiO/SBA-15. This support was selected for its superior performance, attributed to its ordered pore structure, promoting uniform NiO distribution, faster kinetics, and improved redox stability. The optimized material underwent a three-step chemical looping process: (1) reduction of NiO/SBA-15 in hydrogen to Ni/SBA-15; (2) reaction with NO, SO 2 , and H 2 S, forming corresponding oxides/sulfides; (3) regeneration in air to restore NiO. Thermogravimetric analysis exhibited a ~140% increase in H 2 S uptake against NiO/SiO 2 , with stable performance sustained over 10 cycles. Enhancement for SO 2 and NO increased by ~67% and ~316%, respectively. X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis confirmed complete NiO regeneration after 10 cycles. Fixed-bed reactor studies aim to assess the reactivity and pollutant capture efficiency under more realistic conditions. Additional characterizations are employed to understand the influence of morphology on reactivity. This study establishes NiO/SBA-15 as a promising oxygen carrier for integrated pollutant removal.

topic: Advanced Hydrogen Generation Via Thermochemical Water Splitting Using Sol-Gel Synthesized La-Based Perovskite
title: Advanced Hydrogen Generation Via Thermochemical Water Splitting Using Sol-Gel Synthesized La-Based Perovskite

abstract: Thermochemical water splitting (TWS) is a promising pathway for sustainable hydrogen (H₂) production, utilizing redox-active materials to drive oxygen release and reoxidation cycles. In this study, four La-based perovskite compositions LaMnO₃, La₀.₈Sr₀.₂MnO₃, La₀.₈Sr₀.₂Mn₀.₇Mg₀.₃O₃, and La₀.₅Sr₀.₅Mn₀.₉Mg₀.₁O₃ were synthesized using the Sol-Gel method and calcined at 850°C to evaluate their suitability for high-temperature TWS processes. Structural, chemical, and physical characterizations were conducted, including XRD, SEM, FTIR, TGA and optical density to understand the impact of doping and synthesis on redox behaviour. The perovskites underwent thermal reduction by releasing oxygen (O₂) at high temperatures and were subsequently reoxidized with water vapor to generate H₂. The results highlight the critical role of dopant composition and crystal structure in enhancing redox kinetics and hydrogen yield. This work provides key insights into the development of efficient, thermally stable perovskite catalysts for scalable solar-driven hydrogen production.

topic: Thermo-Catalytic Decomposition: Hydrocarbon Feed, Carbon Catalyst Structure, and Regeneration Comparisons
title: Thermo-Catalytic Decomposition: Hydrocarbon Feed, Carbon Catalyst Structure, and Regeneration Comparisons
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Thermo-catalytic decomposition (TCD) activity and stability depend upon the initial carbon catalyst structure. However, further transitions in the carbon structure depend on the carbon material (structure and composition) originating from the TCD process. In this article, reaction data are presented that illustrates the time-dependent TCD activity as TCD-formed carbon contributes and then dominates conversion. A variety of initial carbon catalysts are compared, including sugar char, a conductive carbon black (AkzoNobel Ketjenblack), a rubber-grade carbon black (Cabot R250), and its graphitized analogue as formed and partially oxidized. Regeneration of carbon catalysts by partial oxidation is evaluated using nascent carbon black as a model, coupled with subsequent comparative TCD performance relative to the nascent, non-oxidized carbon black. Activation energies for TCD with nascent and oxidized carbons are evaluated by a leading-edge analysis method applied to TCD. Given the correlation between nanostructure and active sites, two additional carbons, engine soots, are evaluated for regeneration and dependence upon nanostructure. Active sites are quantified by oxygen chemisorption, followed by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). The structure of carbon catalysts is assessed pre- and post-TCD by high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM). Last, energy dispersive X-ray analysis mapping (EDS) is carried out for its potential to visualize oxygen chemisorption.

topic: Isoprenol Dehydration for Jet-Fuel Production: The Effect of Acid Type and Strength
title: Isoprenol Dehydration for Jet-Fuel Production: The Effect of Acid Type and Strength
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Biomass-derived 1,4-dimethylcyclooctane (DMCO), a cyclic alkane, has the potential to serve as a low-carbon, high-performance jet fuel blendstock that may enable jet fuel made with 100% bio-based aviation fuels. Isoprene, the DMCO precursor, can be produced from dehydration of isoprenol, which is obtained by sugar fermentation. In this study, the effects of acid type and acid strength on isoprenol dehydration were investigated with a wide range of solid acid catalysts using alumina, supported phosphoric acid, phosphotungstic acids and organosulfonic acids. It was found that Brønsted acid site favors the dehydration, as high selectivity to isoprene (80-90%) was obtained using a wide range of Brønsted acid catalysts at reaction temperatures from 200 to 300℃. In contrast, Lewis acid site favored isoprenol cracking, as isobutene was the main production from alumina, a Lewis acidic catalyst. While the effect of Brønsted acid strength on isoprene selectivity was minimal, low catalyst acids strength slowed catalyst deactivation, as supported phosphoric acid with the lowest acid strength among the catalysts showed relatively slow deactivation. The findings provide an efficient strategy for isoprene production utilizing solid Brønsted acid catalysts.

topic: Effect of Extraction Solvent on Biocrude Yield, Fuel Quality, and Chemical Composition Derived from Hydrothermal Liquefaction of Lignosulfonate
title: Effect of Extraction Solvent on Biocrude Yield, Fuel Quality, and Chemical Composition Derived from Hydrothermal Liquefaction of Lignosulfonate
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Lignosulfonate lignin, a byproduct of the sulfite pulping process, is a promising hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL) feedstock due to its high water solubility and widespread availability. However, an ongoing challenge in lignosulfonate HTL is the selection of an appropriate separating solvent, which significantly influences biocrude yield and quality. Literature reports yield variations of up to 20% depending on the solvent used, highlighting the critical role of solvent properties such as polarity and water miscibility. Studies also used different separation methods for solvents with lower water miscibility, such as toluene and dichloromethane, and higher water miscibility, such as tetrahydrofuran, ethyl acetate, and methyl ethyl ketone. Considering the widespread compound distribution of lignosulfonate lignin-derived biocrude, the solvent selection is expected to be even more impactful. This study systematically investigates the effect of four solvents: toluene, dichloromethane, ethyl acetate, and methyl ethyl ketone on biocrude recovery from lignosulfonate HTL at 270–310°C with a 30-minute retention time. The solvents were chosen based on their varying relative polarity (2.4–4.7) and water miscibility (0.5%–27.5%), and biocrude was separated using identical separation methods. The results indicate that biocrude yield increases with solvent polarity, highlighting the role of solvent-biocrude interactions in recovery efficiency. Higher polarity solvents reduce carbon and hydrogen content while increasing oxygen, lowering HHV, and shifting toward oxygenated compounds. Boiling point distribution and GC-MS analysis reveal variations in volatility, molecular weight, and compound composition based on the solvent used. These findings emphasize the importance of solvent selection during biocrude extraction for optimizing yield and biocrude properties to meet fuel application requirements.

topic: Catalytic Conversion of Glycerol for Sustainable Production of Solketal
title: Catalytic Conversion of Glycerol for Sustainable Production of Solketal
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: In the biomass conversion and biorefinery sector, turning glycerol into valuable chemicals is an alluring process. This work used glycerol and acetone as raw materials to explore ultrasound-assisted solketal synthesis in a novel way using modified sulfated zirconia as a catalyst. Glycerol conversion was examined by varying three different parameters: reactant ratio, catalyst dosage, and ultrasonic voltage. While synthesizing the catalyst Zr-S-400, different acid concentrations were used, and the catalyst was characterized by FESEM, EDAX, XRD, and Ammonia TPD technique. To maximize the conversion of glycerol, three parameters i.e., reactant ratio, catalyst dosage, and ultrasonic voltage were optimized using Design-Expert Version 13. The reaction mixture was analyzed by Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrophotometer (GCMS). At optimized conditions, maximum conversion (94%) was obtained with 91.5% solketal selectivity. It was found that sulfated zirconia could be reused for up to 4 cycles without significant loss in the catalytic activity. A scale-up investigation for the ultrasound-assisted synthesis of solketal with sulfated zirconia acting as a catalyst was also discussed. The kinetic data was used to scale up the reaction in a constant volume batch reactor model.

topic: Expanding Lewis Acid Zeolites to Determine Zeolite Impact on Selectivity
title: Expanding Lewis Acid Zeolites to Determine Zeolite Impact on Selectivity
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Catalyst selectivity is critical for reducing waste and increasing process efficiency, making it critical to understand how catalyst structure is connected to activity and selectivity. In porous materials, the pore itself can impact the formation of certain products based upon steric constraints. Microporous materials like zeolites are particularly adept at this and these so-called shape selectivities have been largely studied in Brønsted acid zeolites. Yet, we currently lack similar insights for Lewis acid zeolites. A primary issue is that only a handful of zeolites have been made into Lewis acid zeolites despite 256 frameworks and many Lewis acid metals. Sn zeolites are promising Lewis acid zeolites with excellent conversion for epoxide ring opening (ERO) reactions. The selectivity in this reaction is key, yielding a terminal ether or terminal alcohol. With different use cases (polyether polyols for terminal ethers and epoxide oligomerization for terminal alcohols), it is important to understand the causes for selectivity so that they may be tuned. Specific Lewis acid zeolites, Sn-Beta and Sn-MFI, are both highly selective for the terminal ether when the epoxide is epichlorohydrin. As the bulkiness of the epoxide increases however, Sn-Beta becomes more selective for the terminal alcohol and Sn-MFI becomes unselective. These selectivity differences could be attributed to the different pore/ring sizes of the two frameworks, but without other materials to test out this hypothesis, the shape selectivity is hard to identify. In our ongoing work, we present a synthesis for a novel Lewis acid zeolite, Sn-FER. This zeolite is tested using similar reactions as Sn-Beta and Sn-MFI to demonstrate that the ring size affects the selectivity. Overall, the work adds a critical dimension to control the reaction selectivity.

topic: The Role of Gallium Speciation in Zeolites on Methanol-to-Hydrocarbon Tandem Catalysis
title: The Role of Gallium Speciation in Zeolites on Methanol-to-Hydrocarbon Tandem Catalysis
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: The growing demand for light olefins necessitates the development of more efficient and sustainable catalytic processes. Zeolites, with their tunable acidity and shape selectivity, are widely used in hydrocarbon upgrading, where aluminum associated Brønsted acids typically serve as the active sites. However, incorporating less acidic heteroatoms has emerged as a strategy to tune their activity and influence reaction pathways. In this presentation, we discuss our recent work showing how combining gallosilicates and aluminosilicates with distinct zeolite pore topologies (e.g., MWW, CHA, MFI) in a dual-bed reactor enhances production of olefins in the methanol-to-hydrocarbons (MTH) reaction. This configuration uses the less acidic Ga-zeolite upstream as a highly effective dehydration catalyst to convert alcohols to intermediates for downstream upgrading using the Al-zeolite. Here we will discuss recent efforts to elucidate the judicious pairing of zeolites on the basis of Ga speciation and its impact on catalytic performance. To this end, we have used different methods to control gallium speciation via direct synthesis and post-synthesis treatment wherein we assess their performance in tandem MTH reactions with a fixed Al-zeolite (ZSM-5) downstream to establish more robust structure-performance relationships. We have shown that higher Ga loadings promote extra-framework Ga species that suppress C–C coupling, leading to preferential formation of dimethyl ether (DME), while lower Ga loadings with reduced extra-framework Ga promote hydrocarbon production akin to Al-based zeolites. Additionally, we examined the influence of gallium oxide species deposited on siliceous zeolites and mesoporous silicates (benchmark materials). We observed exclusive DME formation over a broad range of Ga loadings, confirming their inability to facilitate hydrocarbon formation. By systematically controlling gallium speciation, this work provides new insights into how different Ga sites influence catalytic pathways in MTH chemistry. Understanding these relationships improves the design of multifunctional zeolites with precisely tailored properties, achieving more versatile and efficient catalysts.

topic: Rapid Synthesis and Control of AFI-Type Zeolite Crystallization
title: Rapid Synthesis and Control of AFI-Type Zeolite Crystallization
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Synthesizing phase-pure zeolite materials with controlled morphology, porosity, and framework composition is critical for advancing applications in adsorption, separations, and catalysis. Zeolite SSZ-24 (AFI-type) is particularly attractive due to its large, one-dimensional 10-membered ring channels that offer high diffusivity and shape selectivity. However, its synthesis remains challenging due to slow crystallization kinetics, narrow synthesis windows, and a tendency to form siliceous frameworks that resist heteroatom incorporation. In this presentation, we discuss a comprehensive investigation of AFI crystallization using both seeded and non-seeded hydrothermal synthesis routes. Systematic studies revealed the importance of silica source selection, organic structure-directing agent (OSDA) concentration, and NaOH content in achieving phase-pure AFI within 48 hours in the absence of seeds—significantly faster than multi-week syntheses typically reported. This rapid, seedless route was enabled by the use of colloidal silica which offered optimal particle size and composition when paired with tuned ratios of OSDA/Si and NaOH/Si. Time-resolved analyses using XRD, SEM, TEM and AFM revealed a two-stage growth mechanism: initial nonclassical transformation of an amorphous precursor, followed by a classical layer-by-layer process of crystal surface growth. Seed-assisted syntheses using different zeolite crystal structures as seeds (e.g., CHA, FAU, and AFI) demonstrated distinct nucleation kinetics and selective templating behaviors, which were further supported by computational studies probing interfacial compatibility and energy landscapes. In parallel, the incorporation of heteroatoms (e.g., Al, B, and Ga) into the AFI framework was evaluated. Our findings revealed that Al and Ga promoted the crystallization of competitive phases (e.g., CHA), whereas boron was introduced into the AFI lattice without compromising crystallinity or porosity. Furthermore, textural analysis confirmed that B-AFI retained high micropore volume and BET surface. Overall, this study advances our mechanistic and synthetic insights into AFI crystallization and provides a rational design approach for tailoring its properties for diverse applications.

topic: Ni/HZSM-5 Nanosheets Bifunctional Catalysts for Hydrodeoxygenation of Lignin-Derived Phenolics
title: Ni/HZSM-5 Nanosheets Bifunctional Catalysts for Hydrodeoxygenation of Lignin-Derived Phenolics
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Lignin is the second most abundant biopolymer in nature and accounting for 15 to 35 wt.% of lignocellulosic biomass. Approximately 50 million tons of lignin are produced annually as a byproduct. The rich aromatic constituents in lignin are great resources for biochemicals and biofuel production. To produce commodity chemicals or fuels, lignin is first depolymerized by breaking the C-C and C-O bonds. Small oxygen-rich molecules are then generated. It is necessary to reduce the O content to a very low level before end use. Phenolics, such as phenol and guaiacol, are among the small O-rich molecules in the depolymerized products from lignin. In this research, Ni/ HZSM-5 nanosheets bifunctional catalysts are explored for hydrodeoxygenation (HDO) of lignin derived phenolics. Ni is active for hydrogenation and hydrogenolysis while the Bronsted acid sites in HZSM-5 are active for elimination and alkylation. Hierarchical MFI zeolites with high mesoporosity and external surface area in bifunctional catalysts enhance performance by improving acid site accessibility. Mesopores enable faster removal of partially polymerized reactants and reduce coking. In this project, we develop the bifunctional catalysts with different structures to evaluate the control of molecular transport towards product distribution tuning. With conventional hierarchical structure, both small and large molecules preferentially diffuse through mesopores. We aim to achieve a novel catalyst structure, in which smaller molecules preferentially diffuse out through the zeolitic pores, achieving a higher yield towards these molecules. The bifunctional catalysts are synthesized with different Si/Al molar ratios in the zeolite and various Ni loadings. Catalytic tests are conducted to understand the catalytic performance difference between the differently structured catalysts and the influence of zeolite chemistry and metal loading. Comprehensive material characterization is conducted on the optimal catalyst. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) are utilized to investigate the chemistry, morphology and crystallography of the catalysts. These characterization techniques will enhance the understanding of the catalysts’ chemistry, structure and performance relationship.

topic: Development and Characterization of Highly Mesoporous Magnetic-Silica Aerogel Nanostructures and Their Role in Enzyme Immobilization
title: Development and Characterization of Highly Mesoporous Magnetic-Silica Aerogel Nanostructures and Their Role in Enzyme Immobilization
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Major challenges associated with enzyme catalysts are their high cost and single-use nature. To address these issues, immobilized enzyme systems have gained significant attention. With increasing interest in nanoparticles, magnetic nanoparticles have emerged as promising enzyme supports due to their advantages such as easy recovery, low toxicity, and high stability. However, bare magnetic nanoparticles are prone to oxidation and aggregation, making surface modification essential. Highly porous SiO 2 materials are excellent candidates for surface modification to prevent oxidation and aggregation of magnetic particles. Additionally, they provide a high surface area, tunable pore size, large pore volume, and ease of functionalization. The development of highly mesoporous magnetic-silica aerogel nanostructures for enzyme immobilization provides several advantages, such as easy recovery from the reaction medium, a high surface area for functionalization and strong enzyme binding, increased enzyme loading capacity, and enhanced stabilization of the enzyme-matrix system. This study aims to evaluate the enzyme immobilization efficiency of highly mesoporous magnetic-silica aerogel nanostructures prepared with different modifications. Magnetic particles were synthesized via the co-precipitation method. To examine the effects of surface area, pore size, pore volume, and hydrophobicity on enzyme immobilization, silica aerogels were prepared using supercritical CO₂ drying with various modifications. BET analysis confirmed that the magnetic-silica aerogel nanostructures possess a highly mesoporous structure, with surface areas of 500–700 m²/g, pore diameters of 11–23 nm, and pore volumes of 2.5–4.2 cm³/g. Enzyme immobilization was conducted using the physical adsorption method, and immobilization efficiency and activity were evaluated. The support materials were characterized using X-ray Diffraction (XRD), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), Fourier-transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), Nitrogen Adsorption-Desorption Isotherm Analysis (BET and BJH methods), and Vibrating Sample Magnetometry (VSM). These findings suggest that magnetic-silica aerogel nanostructures are promising candidates for industrial enzyme applications, offering enhanced stability, and catalytic efficiency.

topic: Leveraging Perovskite Materials for Optimized Energy Conversion and Catalysis of Biomass
title: Leveraging Perovskite Materials for Optimized Energy Conversion and Catalysis of Biomass
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: This study investigates the application of perovskite materials in advanced technologies to improve efficiency and sustainability within the petroleum sector. By leveraging their unique properties, the research aims to enhance energy conversion efficiency, reduce solar energy costs, and improve catalytic processes. The study employs multidisciplinary methods, including the synthesis and characterization of perovskites through solution-based techniques and vapor deposition, and device fabrication for solar cells, sensors, and catalysts. Preliminary results indicate that perovskite based solar cells achieve high power conversion efficiencies at lower costs, potentially increasing solar energy accessibility. Perovskite catalysts exhibit superior activity, selectivity, and stability in hydrocarbon processing, enhancing process efficiency. In environmental monitoring, perovskite-based sensors show high sensitivity in detecting harmful gases, promoting safer industrial practices. The materials also demonstrate excellent corrosion resistance, extending petroleum infrastructure lifespan, and offer promising energy storage solutions for off-grid operations. This research provides novel insights into perovskites' potential to revolutionize petroleum refining and monitoring, contributing to a more sustainable and cost-effective industry.

topic: Synthesis and Characterization of Mesoporous Basic Catalysts from Biomass Waste for Application in Biodiesel Production
title: Synthesis and Characterization of Mesoporous Basic Catalysts from Biomass Waste for Application in Biodiesel Production
session_title: Poster Session: Catalysis and Reaction Engineering Division
abstract: Heterogeneous catalysis has been extensively explored for biodiesel production due to its efficiency and reusability. In this study, three basic heterogeneous catalysts were synthesized via the wet impregnation method, using corn husk ash (Zm)—rich in SiO₂—as the support, and calcined sururu shell powder (Mc)—rich in CaCO₃—as the active component. Both Zm and Mc were thermally treated at 800 °C to obtain SiO₂ and CaO, respectively. The resulting catalysts were characterized by BET surface area analysis, X-ray fluorescence (XRF), X-ray diffraction (XRD), Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA/DTG), and basic strength using the Hammett indicator method. The characterization confirmed the successful incorporation of CaO into the mesoporous SiO₂-rich support, imparting basic properties, as verified by the basicity tests. BET analysis revealed a mesoporous structure (pore sizes ranging from 19.35 to 35.71 nm), with the Zm-Mc30 sample showing the highest surface area (11.91 m²/g). XRF results indicated increased SiO₂ and CaO contents after calcination, while XRD patterns suggested the partial crystallization of previously amorphous silica. FTIR spectra confirmed the presence of Si–O–Si and Si–O–Ca functional groups. TGA/DTG analysis showed similar thermal stability among Zm-Mc10, Zm-Mc20, and Zm-Mc30, with the most significant mass loss occurring near 760 °C. Overall, the findings demonstrate that low-cost agro-industrial residues can be effectively reused to produce basic heterogeneous catalysts, contributing to the development of more sustainable biodiesel production processes.
